Sometimes I even miss phone calls.  For complicated personal reasons, it is extremely critical that I am able to respond immediately to texts or phone calls.This watch vibrates every time I get a text, an email, or a phone call on my phone. Even when my phone is silenced, the alerts come to the watch.  And it vibrates very powerfully.  You cannot miss it.  And not only that, it displays the incoming text on the face of this watch.  How cool is that?  You can be sitting in a meeting, have your phone totally silenced, and casually glance at your watch to read an incoming text message.  There is an even an app (Glance) to send a pre-worded short response.It also displays incoming emails and the Caller ID of incoming phone calls.  You can even read your incoming email on this watch.This watch has way more applications for Android phones than it does for iPhones, which is probably a first.And then there are the watch faces.  There are a bunch of great third party sites where you can design your own watch face!  So, for example, you can download any photo or symbol or logo (whatever you can think of) and render it into a black and white watch face.  Then you can overlay an analog or digital timepiece, and overlay any text or the date (in any format).  The possibilities are endless.Use your corporate logo on a watch face and your co-workers will be putting a Pebble on their Wish List.There are zillions of really cool apps to go along with the Pebble.  An app called Glance will display the weather, show you any calendar appointments you have in the next five days, display stock information, and much more.This does have an alarm function.  It does not beep, it vibrates.You can also control your phone's music player from the Pebble.I have really pushed the envelope on this thing since I bought it a few weeks ago, and found its shortcomings.  The Pebble has a limited memory and only hold about six watch faces or apps at one time.  I also kept adding and deleting watch faces and apps so much I locked up the watch.  The "white screen of death".  I have had to reset to factory default a couple times as a result of this, and then had to reload the custom apps/watch faces.There are times, too, if you fiddle around too much, when you will have to unpair the Bluetooth connection and then pair your phone and watch back together.  There are lots of good online discussions to walk you through any problems with the Pebble you might encounter.The software has recently been upgraded to version 2.0 for the iPhone, but the 2.0 for Android is not yet released.  Some online Pebble apps are already written to the 2.0 version, so watch for that.  They won't work with your Android phone and Pebble yet.  One of the watch face sites I have used a lot has already switched to 2.0 and I did not notice.  It was driving me crazy that the latest watch face I had made was not uploading to the Pebble even though the software said it had.You will love this watch.  It does have a slight learning curve, but man oh man you will love this watch!  Geek heaven!UPDATE: Pebble 2.0 for Android has now been released, and I was able to upload the watch faces I had made.

reviewText: I love this watch.  Simple yet useful alerts keep me connected without being glued to my phone.Plus, I get many compliments and love the customizable watch faces.

The Pebble is a very handy piece of technology, and will continue to develop as such, as more app developers integrate it into their apps. Already, it is extremely useful if you work in a job where you are unable to pull out your phone to check whether or not the message you got was idle chit-chat, or something of actual importance. I really want to give this watch a 5 star rating, but I can't do it.  It may not be fair that I have a Nokia Windows Phone and Pebble does not support Windows phones, but I'm taking that into account and if I was rating on functionality, I would give it a 2 star rating.  The problem is both with Pebble and Microsoft.  I want a smart watch, but due to security limitations with WP8, we may never see a fully functioning smart watch for WP8.  The Pebble seemed to be the most promising with 2 apps that support some functionality.The reason Windows Phone 8 won't work with Pebble or other smart watches:- Microsoft will not allow SMS messages or Phone calls to be intercepted by any 3rd party app.  One Microsoft employee stated on a forum that this was a problem with Android's security model and to protect the privacy of WP8 users, they will not allow access to these API's (even if a phone user want's to grant this permission).  Also, WP8 doesn't really have background applications.  It has a scheduling agent that allows apps limited functionality to do some tasks periodically.- Pebble will not release the low level communication protocol for the bluetooth endpoints.  This limits developers to using the libraries Pebble develops (currently only iOS and Android).  A couple developers reverse engineered the protocol and were able to create two apps, but they are very limited.What can you do with WP8 and Pebble (if you pay $3 for two apps):- Update firmware.- Install watch faces and apps.- Get calendar notifications (only if lock screen is disabled and app is running).- Control Music (lock screen disabled, app running)- Twitter feeds (lock screen disabled, app running)- Phone battery status (lock screen disabled, app running)- Update time- Network alerts (lock screen disabled, app running)- Send some sample notifications, if someday Microsoft opens the SMS and Phone notifications.Pros with the watch:- I think it looks elegant.  It's not as big and bulky as it looks in the pictures.- I like the ability to change my watch face.- The backlight works well and with a flick of the wrist.- It's faster than I expected, probably because I was expecting e-ink, like the Kindle (this is not e-ink).  e-ink is very slow to refresh and this is fast because it is really an LCD screen.  e-Paper is a technology that is very low power and easy to read without a back light, but it is not the same as e-ink.- It's more sturdy than I expected for a plastic watch.Cons with the watch:- The buttons are a little hard to push and feel clunky.- I was expecting e-ink.  I'm not that disappointed, e-paper is faster.- It's a little difficult to navigate the watch, probably because the buttons are hard to push.- It only holds 8 apps/watchfaces- Not an open development framework.  Development is very tightly controlled, it appears.- Straps are actually attractive, but not what you would expect for a $150 watch.- Charging cable is magnetic, but still needs to be tinkered with to make sure it is aligned.

I love the fact that this thing is waterproof.  I don't have to worry at all about getting it wet in the rain or when I wash my hands. Reading my emails while I'm in the shower is so cool!  Battery life is great.  I'll usually get nearly a week on one charge.I think I'll give this one away to a family member and upgrade to the Steel in the future.  That's my only gripe about this watch.  It can look a little cheapo... especially when compared to the newer Steel line.

I have had a black Pebble for a week.  Overall, I really like it, and it does everything advertised on the Pebble site, but I am a person who needs the basic, limited functions the Pebble offers.  It easily paired with my Galaxy S3 phone, using bluetooth 4.0.Connectivity: I can connect with my phone anywhere in my 1 story 1300 sq ft house, but once I walk out the front door, the signal drops. In the last 7 days, it has been super reliable and never dropped the phone's signal except when out of range.There are only 30-40 apps so far, and they are limited because the Pebble is controlled by only 4 buttons and does not have a touch sensitive screen and does not run Android independently.  I can't browse the web, but It does everything I need it to do: displays incoming emails, texts, caller id, and other phone alerts.  Like others, I love being able to SILENCE my phone, leave it in my pack, and not have to worry about missing anything.  It is far more conducive to sharing time with friends than pulling out a phone that beeps every time I get an email- which I feel compelled to check even though it's mostly useless ads.  Any smartwatch will do that, though: the Pebble just fills the bill at the lowest price point.  I am hard on watches and did not want a big investment while I tried out the smartwatch concept- I paid $150 at Best Buy last week, the standard price.  I don't know why sellers are charging so much more on Amazon.Comparing other smartwatches: If you like your watch to stand out, don't get the Pebble.  It is the Anti-Rolex.  It is simple, clean, and a bit elegant while a tad chunky.  It is all plastic and does not look as expensive or draw as much attention as a metal watch or watch with a bright color display.  Not to rip it, but if other people never saw the incoming texts or other trick functions, they might think you paid $30 for it at Ross Dress for Less Outlet.  The watch face is NOT mineral glass, and scratches somewhat easily, so get a screen protector.  The simple black and white display is much easier to see in sunlight than my Galaxy S3, though.  If you want more smart phone functions the Geak Watch (yes, Geak), which runs full Android 4.X, speaker + mike and has wi-fi built in.  Or the durable/multipurpose waterproof microphone/speaker Kreyos watch (this would have been my pick if it were available today).  Or the Omate TrueSmart, which is a veritable smartphone on the wrist. Most smartwatches are still on the ugly side, but the wild, curvy bracelet style Emopulse has the most hypertech bling by far. It is truly amazing and you should check it out. These watches will make the Pebble look very limited in comparison and the Pebble team will have to have a Pebble TWO to compete or go under soon.  So if you can wait, you will certainly benefit. The Sony SW2, which will be released in early October 2013, is a very worthy competitor that will be lighter and slimmer than the Pebble.  It would make a better dress watch, has a few more apps, more flexibility due to the touch screen, and Sony quality control. I like it a lot and I was going to buy it, but found out that it is not as waterproof as the Pebble and has much worse battery life.  The Galaxy Gear is definitely far more advanced than the Pebble and the Sony, but is compatible with very few phones, too heavy, expensive, and has horrible battery life.Many of these "about to be released" watches may also suffer initial quality control problems, further delaying purchase.  While the Pebble is not issue-free, and least the issues are pretty much known as people have using them a few months now and are very vocal on the forums.The Pebble site lists the battery life is about 7 days with average use.  I have not had to charge it yet and I read about 20 emails, 5 texts, three reminders, and screen about 10 calls per day. So it seems very efficient because of its EInk display and more efficient bluetooth 4.0. One gripe, though, it that it does not store any old messages, texts, etc.  It seems to purge everything right after I read it.I measured the main unit at about 1.2 cm thick, 5.1 cm tall, and 3.4 cm wide.  Despite its size, it is light and fairly comfortable. I thought the brightly colored Pebbles (like the red one), made the screen look smaller and accentuated the plastic appearance.  The black case blends in with the display and gives the illusion of a larger display.Beware of screen problems, though: when I am out on a hot day, I get a dark, blotchy-cloudy pattern under the surface of the display (in areas that should be bright white). It does not prevent viewing, but looks bad.  It went away after the watch sat overnight.  This problem is common- see the Pebble forums. Ordering direct from Pebble, they do NOT consider this a defect/reason for refund.  So I highly recommend buying  from a store like Best Buy so you can get your money back, no questions asked.  Personally I decided the cloudiness was not a deal breaker- but if you are a fashionista or particular about the clean look of your electronics it will probably bother you.A Pebble app released in May, "Pebble Dialer" allows you to accept/reject incoming calls from the watch, but I have not tried it.  With a bluetooth headset, or just ear buds, this is a killer feature for taking calls while driving.  Coincidentally, if you go to Google Play and search for Pebble Dialer, you will see pretty accurate pictures of the blotchy display problem.Some apps you might think would be included, well, aren't.  There is no indicator, alarm, or anything to tell you that you have lost bluetooth contact with your smartphone (in that case, the Pebble is just a watch... if you have silenced your phone, you would be unaware that you are missing messages).  Very poor planning on Pebble's part.  There is no countdown timer for those cookies you are baking, nor a stopwatch function.  Perhaps the MOST useful would be a function to use the Pebble to locate a lost phone: a button sequence to press that would make your phone sound a loud ring or alarm noise when you lose it (mine is so slim, it slips between couch cushions very easily)!But the biggest benefit of the Pebble (or ANY smartwatch that is NOT an independent mobile phone) is not so obvious and almost never discussed: minimizing radiation damage. Now I can carry my phone farther away from my body, inside my backpack or briefcase, vastly reducing exposure via the inverse squared law.  While the jury is still out about radiation exposure, cancer, and other hazards from cell phones, the Pebble seems to be very wise insurance. Carrying any cell phone on my body more than an hour per day seems like a very bad gamble. Combine that with being able to silence my phone while spending time with friends, and still not miss any messages (the social grace factor) was easily worth $150.  Without the blotchy display, I would have given it 5 stars.
summary: Best smartwatch on a budget but BEWARE of display issues

reviewText: Physical DesignThere's a certain elegance to the Pebble's simple and understated design. I think it's far better looking than, say, the squat and thick Martian Passport smartwatch. The plastic casing feels hollow, though, and the buttons along both sides of the watch face feel a bit mushy, preventing the watch from having a rock-solid feel. The included polyurethane band is decidedly understated, but you can swap in any standard 22mm watchband.The Pebble is available in black, white, red, orange, or gray. On the left side is a single button that brings you to the Menu page, while the right side houses Up, Down, and Select buttons for navigation. Tapping any of the buttons activates the Pebble's backlight, and quick flicks of your wrist also light up the display, which is a nice touch. The watch face is customizable, and at the time of testing there were nine choices that ranged from a standard analog look to a futuristic dot matrix.The 1.26-inch 144-by-168-pixel e-paper display isn't the clearest or sharpest, but it gets the job done. The e-paper should not be confused with E Ink displays you'll find on ebook readers like the Kindle Paperwhite. It doesn't have the same printed look as E Ink displays; instead it's more of a monochrome LCD. As such, viewing angle isn't a full 180 degrees and it becomes hard to read the watch when you look from an angle. The screen is also pretty reflective, and even with the backlight on it can be hard to read in bright outdoor light, unlike E Ink.On the left side are three contact points that connect to the included charging cable magnetically. It's reminiscent of Apple's MagSafe connector, but the magnetic hold is a bit weaker—I could detach it simply by picking the watch up.The Pebble has a waterproof rating of 5 ATM, which means it can be submerged up to 165 feet and has been tested in both fresh and salt water, so you can shower or swim with the watch. The battery is rated for more than seven days of use, and in my several days of testing, the battery never ran out, despite only charging once for about an hour. You can plug the included USB cable into a computer or a wall charger from a smartphone. The only things included in the box are the watch itself and the charging cable.Android and iOS ExperienceThe primary purpose of the Pebble is to make push notifications accessible on your wrist, and the watch is compatible with both Android and iOS devices. You get the same basic functions on both platforms, but setup, notification settings, and features like music playback work differently on Android and iOS. For my tests, I used an Apple iPhone 5 and an Android-based HTC One X+.When we first tested the Pebble, notifications were hit or miss on both platforms, especially if you rely on third-party apps. Now, thanks to enthusiastic third-party development, there are apps that work with your Pebble to push virtually any notification you can think of to your wrist. On top of that, third-party apps enable features like weather updates or sending canned text message replies right from your Pebble.For both platforms, you must first download the Pebble app and pair your phone to the Pebble using Bluetooth. From there, however, the experiences diverge. On initial setup with Android, you need to enable Accessibility Services on your phone to get notifications pushed to the Pebble. During this process, you'll see a somewhat disconcerting message that reads: "Pebble can collect all of the text you type, except passwords. This includes personal data such as credit card numbers. It can also collect data about your interactions with the phone."On Android the Pebble app now supports a wider array of third-party apps, but not all of them work right out of the box. For example, GoSMS Pro disables the default text messaging app's notifications to eliminate redundant notifications, and its own notifications are not supported in the Pebble app. Luckily, thanks to third-party developers, an app like Pebble Notifier can forward pretty much any notification to the smartwatch. Then there are third-party apps like Glance for Pebble, which can push weather updates to your wrist and allow you to send pre-set text replies to your most recent contacts. And for Tasker fans out there, there's even a PebbleTasker app that lets the Pebble trigger automated tasks on your smartphone.Pebble recently launched a new software update for its iOS app, as well as a firmware update for the watch itself. With iOS 7, the Pebble can do even more when it comes to notifications on iDevices. You now have to set notifications to 'banner' style for each alert you want sent to your Pebble, but the watch and iOS now support basically any notification over iOS, including third-party apps like WhatsApp and even Google Maps navigation. I tested the new Pebble software with Facebook and Twitter and received a multitude of new and timely notifications on my wrist.In my tests, notifications were nearly instantaneous on both platforms and trigger a visual alert and a vibration on the watch itself. Pressing the middle button clears the notification, while the top and bottom buttons scroll through the notification. Call notifications show contact information, text messages show contact information and a preview of the message, and emails show sender, subject, and the first few lines of the body. The Martian Passport, to compare, only shows basic caller ID notifications on its tiny OLED screen. On the Pebble, though, there's no way to look back at a notification once you clear it from the watch face, and you can't control the length of time the message remains displayed.Many of the bugs we encountered in our original review have been ironed out. Music control works far more smoothly now, and notifications are speedy and reliable. It's still not entirely perfect, though, and you'll have to be willing to deal with lost connections, crashing apps, and trial and error to really eke the most out of the Pebble.Pebble also released a new SDK with its latest update, meaning developers can now access features that lay dormant within the smartwatch all along. For iOS users, the Pebble now supports Bluetooth LE, so having the multitude of new notification types pushing to your wrist shouldn't have a huge adverse effect on battery life. Pebble apps can now take advantage of the accelerometer in the Pebble itself, opening up new doors for things like fitness apps. Unfortunately, because of Android's shoddy support for Bluetooth 4.0 LE, which is only available in Android 4.3, the Pebble team is focusing its efforts on iOS development for now.ConclusionAs a category, the smartwatch is still in its infancy and despite its many improvements, the Pebble is still more for the avid geek than for the everyday consumer. The growing collection of third-party apps separates the Pebble from its smartwatch competitors and proves that the developer backing is there. New updates for iOS users signal even more features coming down the road, but it still requires some experimentation to get the most out of the device. Smartwatches can be useful for some, but they aren't for everyone—at least not yet. The Sony SmartWatch 2 is another intriguing option and a nice companion device, but it's also a bit too buggy to go mainstream and while Sony boasts over 250 apps, many of them are half baked. The Samsung Galaxy Gear got the most press of any smartwatch this year, but it's simply too expensive, too limited, and too difficult to use. For now, if you're set on hopping on the smartwatch bandwagon, the Pebble is your best bet for its simplicity and growing feature setPlease rate this up if you found this helpful

reviewText: This is a very handy and convenient sidekick to my phone.  I use it with an iPhone and I love that I can see my notifications as they arrive without having to take my phone out of my pocket.  I get a lot of email so this allows me to decide which notifications need immediate action and which I can ignore for now.  The watch vibrates when you get notifications and phone calls.  I used to miss a lot of phone calls because I could not feel my phone vibrate in my pocket; now, I do not miss any calls!  It is very easy to feel the watch vibrate on your wrist.The watch is water resistant and should be resistant up to a very deep depth (a friend had calculated it for me, and I don't remember exactly what the depth is, but it was so deep that you do not even have to worry about ever reaching that depth)!  I have used it in a pool and water park, and the watch was unaffected.  Of course, I did not have my phone near me while I was swimming, so I did not receive notifications during this time.  But at least I could still use it as a basic watch while I was swimming.The bluetooth range is about 30 feet, so you don't always have to have your phone in your pocket for the connection to remain.  It will work a few rooms away.  Unfortunately, if the watch disconnects for whatever reason, there is no built-in warning.  However, there are some watch faces that you can download from the Pebble Store on your phone that will vibrate your watch when the bluetooth disconnects.  In order for that to work, however, that watch face must be running at the time that the bluetooth disconnects in order to be notified that it has disconnected...the watch does not "multitask".  In short, do not rely on receiving a notification from the watch telling you that it has lost the bluetooth connection.  You shouldn't have to worry about connection, however.  Once you get the initial connection when you power on the watch, you will not have a problem maintaining the connection unless you break the 30 ft. bluetooth range.The battery life is fantastic.  The watch lasts me about 5-7 days of all-day use, powered off only at night.  Furthermore, it charges extremely fast; it usually takes about an hour to completely charge from about 10-20% to 100%.  This is probably because the watch does not use a lot of power so it has a very small battery that discharges slowly and charges quickly.The display is black and white.  It has a decent refresh rate, so games from the Pebble Store will run decently considering that it is running on a low-powered watch.  The display is always on, which is a great feature!  Other smart watches have color, LCD displays that use more battery power so therefore the display cannot stay on all of the time.  The Pebble utilizes a low-powered display that may not look as pretty but it is able to stay on all of the time which I think is much more convenient.  The display has a backlight, and there are a few options you can set with the backlight: you can set it to always turn on when you get a notification or push a button, to only turn on when you get a notification or push a button in a low-light setting (recognized via the watch's ambient light sensor), or to never turn on.  You can also set the watch to turn on the backlight when you flick your wrist (so that you can quickly check the time).  I have mine set to only turn on the backlight in low-light settings...this way I save some battery since I am keeping the backlight from turning on when I don't need it to.  I turned off the wrist flick setting since I found that the backlight would turn on when I am going up stairs, moving my arms intensely, etc.The rubber band is comfortable and widely adjustable to many sizes.  You can upgrade to a steel band if you buy the Pebble Steel instead, which is about $100 more than this product.  In my opinion, the rubber is just fine and it does not look tacky or cheap.If you own an iPhone, you may know that the iPhone is much more restrictive with what applications are allowed to do as compared to Android.  Therefore, there is a little bit of extra effort to keep the Pebble working on iPhone.  Almost every time that I power on my Pebble for the day and connect it to my phone, I receive a notification on my phone asking to allow Pebble to communicate with my phone.  Notifications to your Pebble will not work until you accept this message on your phone.  It is a minuscule thing to do once a day, but it is crucial for receiving notifications on your watch, so don't forget to do it!  Sometimes the message will not appear and notifications work just fine.  Other times, the message will not appear and notifications do not work!  To fix this, simply open the Pebble app.  After opening the app, everything should start working as long as you have a bluetooth connection.  To be safe, every day when I connect my Pebble, I open the Pebble app on my phone and then close it.  That should take care of everything.  Just be careful not to completely close the app from the background (on iPhone, double tapping the home button and closing it through the multitasking tray).  If you do this, notifications will not work.  The Pebble app must be open in the background for notifications to be sent to your watch.I have also discovered that there is a preferred order of powering on your devices.  Sometimes I could not get my Pebble to establish a bluetooth connection with my phone.  I found that if you first turn on bluetooth on your phone and then turn on the Pebble, it will connect with no problem.  Sometimes turning on the Pebble prior to turning on bluetooth on my phone caused the devices not to connect.The selection of apps for the Pebble is not extensive, however at the same time I cannot really imagine what else you can do with a watch!  There are a few apps I do use regularly, including Runtastic (which displays the duration, distance, and pace of my workouts on my watch screen), the music app (pre-installed, allows me to skip songs, play/pause, and adjust the phone's volume), a metronome (as a musician, it keeps a pulse on my wrist...it will vibrate to the tempo), alarm (vibrates when time is up), and Tiny Bird (the Pebble equivalent of the Flappy Bird game).There is a very extensive selection of watch faces (the main screens that tell you the time and some other info).  My favorite is Fair Weather, which displays the time, date, the watch's battery life, a graphic icon of the current weather conditions, sunrise and sunset times, moon phase, barometric pressure, humidity, cloud cover, wind direction/speed, and temperature....all on one screen!  This information is updated over the internet through the Pebble app on your phone.  As long as everything is connected, the information will update automatically every hour and will even automatically adjust your location based on your GPS location (if you allow the Pebble app to use GPS on your phone).IN SHORT...this is an excellent companion for my phone and provides many great features and a stylish new look.  I always get compliments on this watch!

reviewText: I bought the Pebble Smartwatch on release weekend to use with my iPhone and from day one have been more than satisfied with it.  It doesn't have as many features as some other smart watches, but what it does, it does well.  My primary use is to see caller ID or Text ID when I am driving to know if I need to pull over to answer/return a call or text for work.  This watch eliminates much of the potential distraction that a phone can cause when driving.  No fumbling for the phone in your pocket or on your hip.  The watch connects to the address book in your phone and gives you caller ID.  It will also show you the content of texts.  It actually works with pretty much any notification on your iPhone.Although I have downloaded one or two Apps for the watch, there are few that are well done so far.  Buy the watch for how it interacts with your phone and phone apps, not for any standalone apps.  The couple of fitness apps that I have for my iPhone display well on the Pebble.The watch works over Bluetooth, so your phone battery does drain more quickly when using the watch.  This issue is much less noticeable on the iPhone 5s than it was on the iPhone 5.I am totally satisfied with my purchase of the Pebble.  It is great at what it does, but don't expect hundreds of uses yet.Pros:Works great for notifications.  Never has missed a notification that should have come through.Caller ID checks address book on your phone and displays name of callerCan read iMessages and texts entirely on the watch.Cons:Proprietary charger.  Micro USB would have been easier.Plastic over watch face scratches pretty easily.  Probably like most watches, but this could be improved in future.Pebble Apps are not plentiful yet.

Nice to have notifications on your wrist.  Screen and battery life are excellent.  If you want to get use to a starter smart-watch until the others come out, this is it and will not break the bank.  If your on the fence, just buy it you will be happy.

To be continued...wish me luck!Pros:+ Really cool to not have to pull my phone out to quickly read a text or email+ Easy setup and updateCons:- A little bulky but understandable as a 1st gen product- Case cracked within 2 weeks with a pretty minor bump into a wall; too fragile!- Customer service is a bit difficult to work throughI love the idea; Apple would be crazy not to release their own version or improve the Nano as a watch to interface with the iPhone.

I pre-ordered my Pebble just after I missed their Kickstarter promo.  I was a little pissed too when they made the watches available at Best Buy before they filled my pre-order, and worse yet, for the same price.  But all of that aside, I am really happy with my Pebble.  I bought it just because I thought it would be cool to be able to change the watch faces.  I didn't even realize how functional it was going to be.  From my Pebble, I get text messages, e-mail alerts, alarm clock alerts, and call alerts (Pebble Notifier).  I can send a call to voicemail from my watch.  I can also change the ring volume on my phone from audible to vibrate to silent (Pebble Phone Ringer), and there is an app I can use to find my phone by making ring (Pebble Plus).  I can send six different pre-typed text messages directly from the watch to anybody in my phone's contact list, along with an option to send an emergency alert to a pre-programmed phone number, complete with my GPS location (Glance for Pebble).  I can also control my phone's camera from my watch (Watch Trigger).  Although I don't use it, I could get news alerts and stock quotes sent directly to my watch as well.  The Pebble is very functional.  I used to miss a lot of my calls because I usually keep my phone on silent.  With the Pebble, I receive almost all of my calls, and because the Bluetooth connection has a fare range to it, I can tell my phone is ringing even if my phone is downstairs, or if my phone is in the car and I am not.  After you pay the $150 for the watch, all of the apps I mentioned above are free.  It takes a little bit to set it up, but if you have any technical inclination at all, you should be able to figure it out.  Basically, you install one version of the app on your phone, and another version on the watch, and that is how the two communicate.  The Bluetooth connection can be a little finicky at times, and the watch band could stand to be longer (that's why 4 and not 5 stars), but other than that I am totally satisfied with my purchase. reviewText: I've gone back and added to the following review:  In theory, this is a great watch with a great concept:  It's sleek, it's face is changeable, and it's supposed to sync with your smartphone's bluetooth so you can receive texts, emails and see who is calling you.  However, the software is completely dodgy and unreliable.  After a couple of days, emails were no longer showing up on the watch.  A few days later, texts disappeared.  Then, the charger blew up (my computer actually ejected it with an error message that said the USB device was using too much power).  After days of no longer being able to charge my watch, it simply died.  I tried to recharge it with someone else's charger but it was too late.  It's dead Jim.  And so apparently is Pebble's customer service which has ignored all of my attempts to contact them.  These guys are obviously in over their heads, being completely unprepared for the demand for their "amazing" new product that clearly was not ready for prime time.  Save your money and wait for the iWatch.Update:  I finally heard from customer service (so they do exist).  They are overnighting a charger to me via Fed Ex.  Also, after trying to charge the phone again with my friend's charger, I pushed all of the buttons randomly and finally my phone came back.  Oh, and now I'm getting emails, texts and phone calls.So, I've added a couple of stars (although I'm still mad that customer service is so not on top of things) and I've decided the watch isn't a total dud.  However, it's still not really worth the expense and I'm sure the future smartphone watches from Apple, Android, etc. will be much better.  Overall, my experience has been disappointing.

Buyers and potential buyers should introduce themselves to IFTTT dot com, and iTunes apps BoxCar 2, Faast, PushOver, iSmoothRun, etc. Comparable apps exist for Android. A little research, and you'll comprehend the unique benefits. For those who don't feel a need to play Dick Tracy by talking into the watch, or tediously trying to peck out a text on a watch (really?? Puhleeeease!), I suspect you'll be quite satisfied with your purchase. Incidentally, you CAN reject or answer a call via a watch button tap. You will need a phone to speak because, well, that's why you have the phone.Notes:(1) Every color of the original Pebble is in stock this morning (2.19.2014), at GetPebble, for the list $150 price. I'd hate to see anyone's wallet jacked by the trickier 3rd party merchants here.(2) The newer Steel version, which costs twice as much, is a pure case of form over substance. The innards are identical, as is the software. The Steel adds a tiny circular LED light; I know of no app which exploits it.Usage Examples:-- I like to keep a running list of my photo shoot locations. Setting up a phony-name (privacy) FourSquare account empowers me to use the FourSquare Pebble app to do so. (You do NOT need the iTunes FS app running in background.) IFTTT, in a hands off manner, via a recipe I set up, then auto-copies that locale & appends it to my EverNote Logs notebook, where a "Photo Shoots" note lives. RealTime updating, at the tap of a button on my wrist. Woot!-- Running in freezing weather, with a Pebble, frees me to glance only at my wrist (no reading glasses req'd) for stats -- without digging for my iPhone5, courtesy of iTunes app iSmoothRun. It plays well with incoming alerts, leaving the screen so I can see an alert, then gracefully returning. The BlueTooth connection also plays well with my LG Tone earbuds so my music continues without hiccups. (This grandmomma's gotta mentally dance if she's gonna physically  prance!)-- When hubby and I are out & about, and decide to try a new place for munchies, the Pebble Yelp app tells me what we want/need to know. Quickly. Efficiently. Too too cool, and uber helpful!-- A dedicated private Twitter timeline, comprised of a handful of carefully picked news sources (those running Bieber or Miley tweets need not apply), combined with BoxCar2 or Faast, keeps me informed throughout the day. The battery takes a hit, so I recharge every 4 days instead of 6.-- The iTunes Dark Sky app sends a rain/snow alert, 10 minutes before precipitation starts. An IFTTT recipe sends tomorrow's weather forecast to my Pebble the prior evening, via the PushOver iTunes app. Other recipes send me precise sunset time at noon each day, and sunrise info the previous evening -- helps me keep track of "the golden hour" per my photography hobby.-- Alerts from InstaGram, StreamZoo, any weather app, VIP emails, txts, and any app on your iPhone you've set to appear on your Notifications screen, hit the Pebble. "Necessary?" Nope, but man oh man, super convenient.There's more, much more, but you get the drift. Bottom-line, as always, = research is your friend.The watch = 5-stars. But the lack of customer service, coupled with the lack of a genuinely informative one-stop webpage or PDF file, mandates a reduction. Fortunately, super helpful folks hang out in the GetPebble dot com forums.
summary: Looks Nice, with its Ultimate Power Found in *Your* Hands

reviewText: I updated this review based on the November 2013 iOS7 update.I bought mine directly from Pebble. I gave this a single star in my initial review because it did flat out not work as advertised for iPhone/iOS. This appeared to be an iOS only problem, but that's what applied to me and what I based teh review on. For the first year or so, email notifications did not work at all (Microsoft Exchange email accound -- which I had no issues with on other devices), caller ID only showed numbers and sometimes not even that(again, for iPhone).As of the November 2013 software update, both email notifications and caller ID work most of the time. Sometimes the notifications are delayed for up to an hour and suddenly appear all at once, even though I've had the phone in close proximity to my Pebble the whole time. There are still several minor but annoying issues that I believe are still iPhone exclusive. For instance, a pop-up that asks me for permission for the Pebble to communicate with the iPhone which appears at random intervals. When using it over time, you get the overall feel that the product isn't well integrated with iOS. Many people (getpebble.com forum posters) blame Apple for the previous and remaining problem, but that doesn't help the end users. Apple doesn't sell this product, and Apple doesn't advertise this product. If Pebble can't get the watch to work for iOS, they should not advertise it as compatible with the iPhone. Period.I also can't use the Pebble with Polarized sunglasses, the screen becomes virtually invisible. Battery life is sometimes down to one day, around 4 hours most of the time. There is also very little warning before the battery dies, and you only get the warning in the setup screen on the watch.In summary, the Pebble has improved dramatically since I got it, and I am actually able to use it now. But given the company's track record for false advertisement and overall lack of response from customers, I will never purchase from them again. Take a look at the forums on getpebble.com and search for customer support response (or lack thereof).I really love the concept (light-weight watch, vs. for instance the Samsung Gear which is basically a shrunken cellphone), but I am disappointed with how the company executed on this idea.
summary: Works OK -- but not more than that (for iOS)

reviewText: Disclaimer: I am a devoted Amazon fan, however I purchased my Pebble at BestBuy, where the price was $150. This is one of the only geek gadgets this year I have purchased outside Amazon, but saving $69/watch (I bought 2) was hard to pass up.Whether you have an iOS or Android smartphone (or tablet - it works with those too) to pair with the Pebble will probably directly relate to how much bang you get for your buck. I have a Samsung Galaxy Mega smartphone with a 6.3" screen which fits comfortably in my purse, however, I don't like constantly taking any phone in and out of my purse every time to check it when I get a text or email (and I get a lot.) This watch not only notifies me who is calling,  it also notifies me who is texting (and what they're saying), who's Facebookin' me, and who is emailing me personally to one address, and emailing me at my separate work address.  For both my personal and work email, the subject and part of the message is displayed on those alerts. Using the Pebble smartwatch app and the 3rd party Pebble Notifier app (both available from the Playstore), this watch frees me up to pull my smartphone out when I want to, rather than have to.The install of the app and upgrade of the firmware thru Pebble's app on the Android o/s is fairly easy - however it isn't straight forward, consistent or user friendly when installing the app or upgrading the firmware for the watch on the iOS 7 o/s.  In fact, the iOS version of the Pebble install/firmware update can be downright annoying: it took twice to install the app and firmware update on the iOS device for the Pebble to finally install the firmware, reboot and reconnect. I can only attribute this to the fact that iOS 7.0 was recently released by Apple and as per their usual modus operandi, they've also released at the same time the SDK's (software developer's kit) necessary for OEM's like Pebble to develop their corresponding AppStore apps. So in short, using the new iOS 7.0 with the Pebble smartwatch app is more buggy than that of the Android version and may continue until developers for the product further their knowledge of the new iOS 7 operating system. It bears noting that extending the inherent watch and Pebble app capabilities via 3rd party apps is more mature and plentiful for Android users vs those with iPhone or other Apple devices.The battery life is terrific - even with heavy use. The watch has a large face - on men this is insignificant, but for women with slender wrists it's noticeably significant. The watch band, thankfully because I'm not much into rubber, can be changed to any 22mm band.All in all, provided you recognize that this device is a first step toward emerging smartwatch technology and the capabilities are different between Android and iOS smartphones/tablets, you shouldn't be disappointed with your purchase.

I ordered my pebble via Kickstarter in July 2012 and got it more than one year (!) later. While the watch now is also available via Amazon.com, unfortunatelly enough, it doesn't seem to ship to Europe.The watch itself is a nice, understated piece of elegant technology. It's one of these things that makes life a little easier. Someone calls? You'll get his/her name on the display and a non-intrusive vibration to go with it. You get a short message? Read it on the little display if you want. Bored with your watch face? Get a new one.But there are still a couple of things to be ironed out. My biggest grief is the battery. Yes, the battery load lasts for about a week, also due to the low power consumption design, which is great for a Smartwatch. But the battery cannot be changed. So in two or three years, I have to throw away the watch and have to hope that there will be a replacement which I still like. This is a major bummer and kind of a "rent a watch for a couple of years" concept instead of "buy a watch and be happy".Second bummer might be the SDK 2.0. Yes, great features and all. But of all the hundreds of watchfaces, you will apparently be only able to use the ones that get adapted for SDK 2.0 as it is not backwards compatible. So if you see nice watchfaces for Pebble that are not very recent, you might be out of luck using them on your updated Pebble.All in all, from a functional point, I'm quite happy with my Pebble and hope that there will be a model that looks very much the same soon that will provide a changeable battery, maybe even with a standard Micro USB port for charging as the charging cable is proprietary and doesn't stick well to the watch. And maybe there could be a "Gorilla Glass" update or something as well which is less prone to scratching.

reviewText: My long anticipated Pebble watch arrived yesterday after I had pre-ordered it in spring. I have a weakness for gadget watches (e.g. this wonderful electromechanical one:Phosphor Men's MD012G Swarovski Mechanical Digital Watch), so the Pebble fits right in the collection.PACKAGEThe wrapping box is nice 'treehugging-cardboard' that resembles the Kindle's box. The first visual impression of the watch is OK: big, bold, sleek and with a black strap. On closer examination its a plastic affair with 4 buttons on the sides. There are some indications of cheap workmanship: In one of the corners of my Pebble the plastic fits poorly leaving a sharp gap. It looks like a $40 digital black watch that vaguely imitates the styling of Swiss RADO. Steve Jobs would not have approved, but it will do for me.Battery life seems good enough (a few days). The Pebble cannot be opened and its battery cannot be replaced. This means that in 5-7 years it will be a piece of chemical waste that must be properly recycled. The practical lifespan will likely be much shorter anyway, given how quickly personal electronics become obsolete.DISPLAY: poorAfter switching the Pebble on the display immediately disappoints. Its smaller than the size of my black Pebble would suggest. The pixels seem large: much bigger than we are used to on E-ink displays in a Kindle or the retina display of Apple Products. As a result the graphics seem quite pixelated. The display does not support greyscale, so any photos look pretty bad.The display is poorly readable in low light due to the dark plastic that covers it. A backlight only briefly lights up when a key is pressed or by vigorously shaking it. During daylight its somewhat better and contrast seems to be decent. And in sunlight is also OK.A major disappointment is that the display becomes almost completely unreadable when wearing (polarized) sunglasses. That means that the display is not actually E-ink. Instead, its a conventional Black-and-White LCD screen. All of Pebble's advertising prominently calls it 'e-paper', but it looks nowhere as good as the e-ink as we know it from the Kindle or Nook. The Pebble uses black-and-white LCD technology just like any other digital watch in the past 30 years. It surprises me that almost none of the reviews picked up on this. Real e-ink watches already exists:Phosphor Unisex DH01 Digital Hour E-INK Curved Polyurethane Band Watch. The advantage of LCD is the faster response time than e-ink, which allows cooler animations in the watch faces. The disadvantage is clearly the visibility.SETUP & USEInstallation and pairing is easy after installing the smartphone app. The app is very nicely designed and simple. Right out of the box, Pebble shows email, text messages and caller phone number/ID. A few watch faces are included that show the time and date. Clicking through them on the watch is easy with the 4 buttons. Otherwise, the settings are limited to just a few basic options.Pressing the buttons requires quite some force and is a little awkward. It seems a little out-dated way to interact with this gizmo. I'm missing a smooth touch screen like the iPod nano which would have made this a more useful tool. The Pebble has a motion sensor, but apart from switching on the backlight I have not yet found an app that used it.SOFTWARE: limited functionality and unstableThe key selling point of the Pebble is its quick notification capability. With every phone call or incoming text the Pebble will buzz and briefly show the information. After a minute or so it switches back to the the clock screen. That is is pretty cool to be able to check this with a quick glance of the eye rather than taking smartphone out of my pocket. I have not found a way to recall previous messages, which is a weird omission.The current iPhone app does not give notifications for Twitter, Facebook or Calendar reminders, which is a big bummer. There are some 3rd party apps that attempt to fill that void, none of which got me exited. The main raison d'etre of Pebble (quick notify at a glance) is quite obviously crippled. To make matters worse, iPhone Pebble app also has a bug that makes it not show any email message notifications beyond the first.There are many apps available made by enthusiastic developers world-wide. You can cycle through some 8 on the phone (which is a little on the small side).  Most of them are watch faces: some cool, some corny, some totally unreadable. A few apps do a little more than just show time and date. To enable internet enabled data such as weather or traffic info, a second app 'httpebble' must be open on the smartphone. Its a little strange that that is not included in the default pebble app (that also must be running). The apps that are using httpebble seemed to be unstable, often loosing connection.I installed quite a few apps. All of them are 'display-only': there is no way to configure them or change app-specific settings. This seems to be a limitation of the Pebble UI setup. For instance, I tried a few apps that show weather where there did not seem to be a way to select the location or a preference for C or F.I tested Pebble with the RunKeeper app. That works fine, but the lack of customization is annoying. I miss being able to select what I want to see, something can is easy on the Garmin GPS watches:Garmin Forerunner 410 GPS-Enabled Sports Watch with Heart Rate MonitorThe process of installing apps is simple but not as smooth as the Apple app store. First you need to go a website in the smartphone browser, click download, and then open it in the Pebble app.  It becomes clear that Pebble needs to work on the stability here.  The install process regularly crashed the watch. Especially the apps that use httpebble to connect to the internet seem to be quite unstable.  After the crash, some previously installed watch apps have disappeared, which is quite annoying.Pebble's stability is a big issue. It crashes a number of times per day on me while scrolling through the watch faces. Pebble also seems to lose the bluetooth connection sometimes. That is annoying since no indication that it was lost. The only way I found to reconnect was to switch Pebble off and on, and once I even had to re-pair it with my iPhone.OVERALLThis is a nice but somewhat flawed gadget that is still very much under development. It does not live up to the high expectations after it went viral on Kickstarter. Pebble still pretty cool now its new, but even with software updates I suspect it will become obsolete rather quickly. That is because the hardware looks (and is) cheap, the screen is rather poor, and the software setup has issues. Apple certainly would not have released this as an iWatch, but for now I enjoy this little toy.Update May 2014: With a new app an new firmware the Pebble has become much more stable and usable. So much so that I'm using this watch daily and crashes have become less frequent. The new iPhone app is easy to use and allows for easy installation of new watch faces. A highlight is the PebbleBucks watchapp that allows me to pay at Starbucks by holding the Pebble in front of the scanner.
summary: Not as advertised: uses LCD instead of E-ink screen

reviewText: I have a problem with my smartphone. Actually most cell phones. Being near 60 and having suffered some mild hearing loss, I don’t always hear it ring. It doesn’t matter if I carry my iPhone 4s in my pants pocket or on my belt in a holster, I miss calls from not hearing it ring. The vibrate mode on the 4s is weak in my opinion, to the point where I don’t always feel the phone when it vibrates from an incoming call. Missing calls is not something I like to do and wearing a bluetooth headset all day in the headquarters of a Fortune 500 company is something that is frowned upon.Smart watches started becoming a reality and I investigated purchasing one. Unfortunately, (or fortunately, depending on how you look at it) due to Apple’s tight, competition unfriendly constrictions, the choices were minimal. This made my search fairly easy.I received the Pebble for Christmas, black case and band. We purchased direct from the website as they offered a discount. I have used it daily since then. It has resolved my issue of missed calls and I actually have some fun now and then in making my own digital watch faces. Since it pairs with the iPhone, I do have it set to use the iPhone’s time for my watch display. As long as the cell provider’s tower is up, the time is good and accurate. It may not be atomic, but in my opinion it is the next best thing while considerably less expensive than an atomic time wristwatch.When a call comes in, my watch vibrates. When I receive a text message or any other notification, my watch vibrates. I can read the watch displayed information when a call is incoming and decide whether I need to fish the phone out of my pocket to answer said call. The Pebble uses the contact ID information from the phone to identify the caller. Text messages and other notifications appear on the Pebble screen. You can scroll down using one of the watch buttons to read lengthy messages. The Pebble does not store these messages, which I don't think is really necessary. The message remains on the phone until you clear it from there.While the font is small, it is sharp and quite readable. I am a fan of Kindle e-readers and e-ink technology, especially when it comes to reading something on a screen in bright sunlight. The face is reflective and I think in future iterations should be made non-reflective like current e-readers. This would improve readability in bright light, but it isn't that big an issue. The backlight comes on with a flick of the wrist and makes reading it in the dark very easy.Pebble has at least one game for the watch, but it isn't my brand of joe so I haven’t tried it. I bought the watch for a specific purpose(s) and playing games on a small screen like this isn’t that purpose.Pebble is still in its infancy (okay, maybe it’s at the toddler stage) and has some growing to do. I’m hoping for some truly useful apps (at least useful to me) in the near future to make use of all the watch’s features.Here are some of the highlights and lowlights I have noted:Pros:Display is very readable, even in bright sunlight.Customizable FacesSimple to UseRange is good to excellent. 30 to 50 feet from the phone and it is still paired.Keeps great time.Cons:Display shows dark splotches on the screen when viewed through polarized lens.Battery meter-no way to tell if the battery needs recharging from the face or from a message. Other devices either have an icon or notification (on the device or via e-mail) when recharging is needed. The Pebble should, too.Waiting for really good apps, like one that can take advantage of the hardware in the Pebble and turn it into something of an activity monitor that can display steps taken, calories burned and other data throughout the day, then store that data for 1-3 days.Initial set-up was somewhat problematic. I think the instructions on the website could have been clearer. Seems that I recall a step or two may have been missing or not clearly explained.While it is almost all plastic and rubber for exterior construction, it probably isn't the sturdiest watch you’ll ever own, but I have no issue with that. My days of needing a rugged, take any form of punishment life can dish out watch have passed. They have recently come out with a steel version. Probably sturdier than the plastic version, but not a problem for me.I’m not overly impressed as yet, but I am happy with the watch. I think it has yet to realize its full potential and I am anxiously awaiting those apps I will use that can fully exploit the watches capabilities.

I got this for my grandson seeing it was on the top of his Christmas list.  He is tech minded to the max and he was delighted with it.  At a birthday party on the 29th.  He showed it off to everyone.  He is a happy Pebble watch owner.  Recommend.

The Pebble is an easy to use smartwatch that provides the information that I need.  I do occasionally have it disconnect, but it is no problem to get it started.  I use the smartstatus app as my watchface and it provides the time, day of the week, month, and date.  Additionally it provides me the current weather to include if it is sunny or cloudy and the current temperature.  It tells me what t percent my battery is on my cellphone and also gives me the date/time of my next appointment and what that appointment is.  This is all on one easy to read screen without having to push a single button.  I like the flick of the wrist to turn on the back light when in a dark setting.  The watch is very light (you hardly know that you have it on your wrist). One morning, I put on my regular analog watch and about an hour later, I went back to my Pebble as I missed the information that was not there.  I may upgrade to Pebble steel as it is much nicer looking, but for now this is my "go to" watch.  I highly recommend this smartwatch.
summary: All the information you need on your wrist

reviewText: The watch does exactly what I needed it to do it lets me know when I get a phone call it lets me know when i get a text that lets me know when I get email it gives me an update on the weather and I really enjoy having it since I have to have my phone on silent most of the time I don't lose out on knowing what I need to know or being able to answer a very important call. It also works much better since the resent software update.

I bought a black and a red Pebble. The black one arrived DOA. Seriously, the watch face had a "sad watch" icon -- meaning these things ship without an quality insurance inspection. The red pebble paired with my iPhone 5S, but had problems pairing with the iPhone 4S.All in all, I think you should just wait until Apple comes out with their own iWatch (this Fall) or get some Galaxy Gear if you an Android user.

The Pebble Smart Watch is a neat gadget to use when you are in a meeting or out to dinner and you want to see a message as it is coming in.  The only drawback is range from where you place your phone.

I'll start with an easy pros/cons:Pros:Easy to setupEasy to useBacklight is the perfect brightnessCrisp display is easy to read most of the timeLong enough lasting batteryCharge connector is easy to useCons:Not a "smart" watch.  More like a "clever" dumb watch.Limited usefulness overall- no touchscreen and only 4 buttons limits the future applications- no real easy way to add apps and faces to it, convoluted process to say the leastThey could have used the middle button to advance to the next notification (both the left and right-middle buttons dismiss the message), but they chose to make you scroll with the up/down button.  Sometimes you end up scrolling into the next message then have to go back and scroll some more.Looks and feels quite cheap... Watch is very expensive compared to the build quality- you can see where the sealant they used squeezed out between the halves of the case.  Don't believe? Look right above the watch strap where the glossy cover meets the textured back.Impressions:After receiving the watch I almost sent it back.  There was quite a bit of glue around the edges of the case and the general overall vibe was that this is an easy to scratch, cheap, hastily assembled watch for the money.  But after trying it  for a few hours it grew on me.  I still think the watch is worth, at most, $50 based on build quality and limited functionality.  But it's convenience makes up for the poor quality and lack of any real beneficial apps.  I have not gotten it wet yet, so I can't speak to its 5 ATM WR rating.I also have a Martian Victory, which is also overpriced for its build quality.  The Martian is great for looks (I use it for work).  The Pebble is good not great for play (water resistant -- i hope --).  I would say the Pebble is great for play, but I don't think the plastic front will withstand some types of play and at anything over $50 in price its a real stretch to call it "great for play".Conclusion:So far there is no truly great "smart" or "clever" watch available for iOS.  If you were hoping for the Pebble to be the first, keep waiting, you will only be disappointed with the Pebble.Update March 8th, 2014:The 2.0 update is out...  Didn't help my Pebble feel any less cheap or plastic ;).  I still don't think this watch is worth $100-$150.  Its now a $69 watch in my mind, up from $50.  The metal one MIGHT be worth $150 if its' vibrate feature doesn't sound like its tearing the phone apart.On the topic of vibration:Since wearing it at work a few days and leaving my Martian at home, I noticed that the vibration notification is so violent that it rattles the buttons and actually causes more of an interruption in a meeting than just leaving the phone's ringer on.  It sounds like it is actually rattling inside too since I can hold all the buttons gently and there is still a rattle noise during notifications.  So I had to set the Pebble's do not disturb to 22:00 - 17:00 so there is only 5 hours a day that the vibration isn't going to be an annoyance to anyone but me or my wife.  Discrete notification is NOT this watch's forte.Software:Version 2.0 is where this watch should have been on 1.0.  Its still sad that all the useful in-watch apps require the purchase(more often)/free download(rarely) of a "helper app" instead of Pebble making a real effort to integrate more functionality into their own app's back end to allow developers the freedom to do it all in one place.  At least there is a single place to go now to find apps/faces for your watch, so I guess that is progress.  Pebble's 2.0 app is kind of flashy graphically, but VERY clunky in operation.  It doesn't remember where you were while browsing the available apps/faces so if you want to check out the details on an app/face you have to resign yourself to going back to the search, typing in your query again, and scrolling to where you left off (if you can remember).I think that gets to the root of the problem with Pebble.  The company seems to have many dreamers, artists, and creative types, with only a few engineers.  Those engineers have no concept of UI design or usability (nor do the artists) so everything kinda comes out looking good with a bunch of quirks that really take away points from the overall experience.  Everything about this watch still feels half-assed and rushed with NO sense of apology about that or any other redeeming qualities.If you've not bought a "smart" watch yet, I'd keep waiting to see what the 3rd generation holds or, if Apple makes one, the 2nd generation after people start copying that.This watch is still 3 stars, just based on the physical appearance and build quality.
summary: Good or Ok are the best ways to describe this watch

reviewText: UPDATE May 20, 2014.  After testing the new firmware update for a few weeks I believe previous pairing issues between my pebble and Mapmyfitness have been solved.  The firmware update was described as addressing connectivity issues with certain fitness apps.  Apparently so.  Therefore, I am upgrading my rating and, feeling generous, I will give it five stars despite the teething issues.  It now does everything I expected of it without hiccups.ORIGINAL REVIEW:  Bought this at a local retailer as I was in a hurry.  So this is not a verified Amazon purchase.  I really want to love and use my red pebble watch.  It looks cool and simplifies my workout experience so much when it works.Therein lies the problem.  It doesn't always pair properly. I am using the Mapmyfitness app on an LG Optimus Pro G cell phone.  Not dated technology.  The watch shows paired to the phone via bluetooth, the phone shows paired to the watch, but it isn't always so.  Sometimes it works fine. Then, sometimes during mid workout, the connection stops - even though it still shows as paired.  I log onto the getpebble.com site and follow their instructions carefully - unpairing, turning both devices off, etc - and they show paired but there is still no connection.Of course sometimes it does pair properly and stay that way for days.Perhaps pairing is better with the iphone?  I don't know but I do know this is very frustrating and I have spent far too much time fooling around with pairing and trying to get the watch to work properly in this regard.I am not super technical but I am not a moron.  I've slaved new drives into my PC, upgraded cards, fans and power supplies etc. so I can follow instructions, am not intimidated by technology, and think I am doing everything correctly to make this work.  Could it be my phone?  I guess so.  Could it be the mapmyfitness software?  I doubt it.  That seems to keep working fine and is certified to be pebble compatible.I really cannot recommend this device given the problems I am having with it. But, because it could be my phone I am giving three stars instead of the two I think it deserves.
summary: Updated review - Firmware Update Fixed Pairing Issues

reviewText: My Pebble was not functional at all for the first few weeks I owned it. The customer help was not a help, but I lingered in returning it and, I have to say, am glad I did. They eventually released an update to the app that allowed the thing to get working. I now can choose the different watch faces it comes with, can use the Run Keeper app on my Android Moto-X, and can get alerts.  I cannot download new faces via My Pebble Faces.  Not sure why, and that's frustrating.Overall, this feels like it's been produced and supported by the smartest kids at Stanford, who would have benefited from more adult supervision. I like the email and phone call alerts, and the Run Keeper app works well. I can't download new faces, and it feels like a good whack will result in a nice scratch on the screen. The Pebble Steel looks great, and unless Google comes out with something better, I'll probably upgrade my Pebble to that in a year or whatever. However, I wouldn't expect great customer support., etc. If you're excited, buy now. Otherwise, wait for the Steel, which will probably have more issues worked out, and which will definitely be a more robust piece of tech.
Very good and dependable

I've haven't worn a watch for a long time, and I am now really enjoying it.  With the pebble, I can turn off the ring on my phone all the time.  Being able to glance at my watch to see my messages is surprisingly convenient.  Not sure how I ever did without it.  I lost one that was given to me as a gift, and immediately ordered a used replacement.

I funded this on Kickstarter. I have had the watch for about 6 months. If I don't get a lot of  messages the batteries last about 7 days before I recharge the watch.The Pebble has evolved several times since I purchased it. Now anything that I allow in Notifications in my Iphone will come in as a message. I can also receive email.  What I like most about the Pebble is I can leave my Iphone on vibrate and still see who is calling, reject the call or answer it. I work as a security officer in a Federal Court house so it is nice that I don't have to worry about the phone going off. I have ordered a Kreyos and a Hot watch but I can say that I am very happy with the Pebble. I have several watches that I would wear including a Hamilton like Elvis wore in a movie in 1956. I now wear the Pebble all the time as even if my phone is at the other end of the house I know that I am receiving a call.  Personally I love this watch. Go Pebble. I also changed my watch band for a leather (wide Band for Pebble)  I am not affiliated with the Pebble company in any way.

I purchased this watch during the "kickstarter" program. It sounded promising with lots of great features, many that work with your iPhone. One of the really neat features I was looking forward to was the ability to see who was calling me by just looking at my Pebble instead having to pick-up my phone. How cool would that be? Well, I did get my Pebble for being a kickstarter supporter, but even after many emails to support and many software updates,  the simple functionality of being able to see your contact name on the pebble for an incoming call is not working. I feel there will be much better options out soon from the major manufacturers that will actually provide a watch that works with good tech support. My recommendation is stay away from this start-up companie's good idea with poor execution.

The Pebble has some pretty great features, and a lot of developer flexibility means more great features on the way.However, I'm having a lot of trouble getting over the feel of this watch.  The buttons are huge plastic protrusions with a ton of play.  Make sure you press directly in the middle of them, or you get nothing!  The charger has some trouble staying attached.  That would be fine if the Pebble gave me a better indicator of battery percentage than it does...I'm going to build an app that will let me use the Pebble exactly how I intended to.  If it's difficult to do, clunky, or anything less than incredible, I will be returning Pebble and waiting for a new challenger.
summary: Cool toy, but feels like a toy.

reviewText: I bought this for myself to use with my iPhone 5.The good- kinda cool being able to get text messages and notices on my watch.  I like having my watch vibrate when I get a phone call in a noisy place.  Nice being able to change the face plates with apps.The bad- Had troubles getting watch to sync with phone. You lose this cord and you are screwed.When battery went dead my phone would not charge back up.  I sent my phone back for refund.  Don't think the product is quite ready yet.
summary: Good idea.  Just not quite ready yet

reviewText: Ordered this and received an open box with a clearly used watch in it,  had several scratches, literature was all wrinkled, power cord not wound etc.  Nowhere in the description of the item I ordered did it say it was not a New item.

This watch is great!  I love being able to try different watch faces every day.  There is an app so that I can even create my own watch face. So I did.  It was easy to load it on an use it.  I added it to the others on my Pebble.I'm hard of hearing.  Normally I need to have my phone on LOUD to hear it even with my hearing aids and sometimes I don't feel the vibrating alert on my phone.  Other times I have my phone in the bedroom because I don't have it with me.  Nevertheless, my Pebble will vibrate and tell me who is calling.  Even 30 feet away.  It is totally awesome.  If I want to ignore the call I just click the button on the watch.For those of you that don't like the Pebble because they think that it looks cheap.  Prior to the Pebble, all of my watches (except the one that I use to work in the yard) were fancy $500+.  I now wear my Pebble everywhere.  I meet with executives, and often I'll show it to them and next thing they want to know what it costs and where to get it.I also wear my Pebble running and occasionally in the shower or bath.  Never a problem.I added the Skinomi Skin to the watch face to protect it.The only drawback is that I'm 55 and find it difficult to read the text messages without my readers on.  I wish that I could increase the font size of the text.  For this reason, and only this, I give it 4 starts.

I was one of the original kick starter backers, so I received one of the first pebble watches in the market, I have gotten to see the growth of the interface and app development along with longest hours of actual daily use comparable to others.This is my take away:PROS:Sleek design and low profile. Most people compliment me on the watch without knowing about pebble or smart watches at all.Choosing watch face, there are so many to choose from and sites that will even let you make your own.. Really cool to explore and change things up.E-ink display, I have gotten to play with the samsung galaxy watch and had attempted the iPod nano watch band before... When your outside trying to see your watch against the glare it's the worst, the e-ink screen is perfect... And the auto light feature when you flick your wrist is so intuitve and natural and really helps in low light conditions. It lights up similar to the new kindle paper white.Battery life, a watch needs to tell the time first before any bells and whistles are added... The fact that one charge lasts a week is amazing. Going away for a weekend trip and not needing an extra charging cable for my watch just seems like a logical thing, but alternatives on the market last barley through a day with heavy use.Open source for developers, means that there is a flood of apps being made and some amazing tricks done with the technology for you to explore... If you like the basic functions it's still worth it, but pro users can really dive into the options out there.Checking your text without digging through your pockets/bag/coat is so helpful. We have notifications hitting us left and right, and you don't want to miss an important one, but it's so frustrating to stop your actions to check the message you got only for it to say "ok"... At a glance you can see your message and continue on your way without breaking a stride.Water proof, huge! I have leather watches that I can't wear out in the rain and this is technology and I can go swimming with it! For those who are active in sports this is a great feature.Great with sport apps, think about the $300 Nike GPS watch and all that nonsense, your phone is an amazing personal computer in your pocket that can measure everything... Let that investment do the work and this screen serve up the details.Controlling your music, sounds silly but I use this all the time when I am in the car or hosting a party... If the song is not that great I can just click my wrist and go to the next one. Also being able to see who is playing is helpful when your in a party with a spotify radio or pandora playing and someone asks the classic "who is this? I love this song" and without pulling out groove shark or running to the iPhone in the dock you can glance at your wrist and respond with confidence.Easy to change watch bands, I have swapped out my watch band several times, it's great and easy.. Using the rubberish one they send for sport activities and swapping to a nice nylon band with some personality when I am going out for the evening.CONS:No image support, this sounds silly with an e-ink display but I wish it would do what kindle does with images and just show in black and white, it's kind of annoying to get a text that is an image and you just get a blank message alert on your watch...Full potential unlocked for the tech savy, meaning that they have not created a seamless environment to get all the wonderful apps and tweaks for it. And to unlock the full potential requires some tech know how.. Not much but for a low tech user they will get basic functions and it's worth it, but can be daunting to know your missing out... They are in the process of making a pebble App Store to address this issue though.Can't respond to text messages, sounds silly but it stinks that you can't generate a basic response from the watch (yes, no, maybe) this might get added in later with updates but for now it's not there and it's a noticeable void in the experience.Notification management, since your notifications or usually subtly hitting your phone with a minor ding/vibrate.. When the vibration is on your wrist as well you will quickly learn its not as important to be told about every Facebook notification or gilt sale... So making sure to manage your apps notifications is necessary.In conclusion:I recommend the watch to all people who ask about it, it can be opened up to do a lot of amazing things like prompting your navigation directions while riding your bike so you can keep your phone in your pocket and safe. Or answering your phone while snowboarding and your helmet has headphones but the the cord is buried in your jacket. It's simple life challenges this watch fixes, and for the price point it's just an amazing looking watch.
summary: Review and findings after 10 months of use

reviewText: Great watch for iphone owners. Only had a problem with the setup, it was harder than it should've been.  What's great about it is I can control my music on my phone and the vibrate on the watch is a lot more discreet than the vibrate on the iphone.  The band is on the cheap side and the upgraded version could include color, sound and I also should be able to talk to the caller on the watch.

I've had a Pebble for about 3 months and in no way can recommend purchasing one for iOS users. It has so much potential but it has been exceptionally buggy and their customer support has been virtually non-existent.A few days after purchasing it, I noticed I had stopped receiving notifications.  I contacted support about it but got no response.  After searching through the forums, I found some other people that had the same problem and the suggestions had been to forget your Bluetooth connection on your phone and re-pair the device.  I ended up doing that on pretty much a daily basis to keep the watch working.  A new firmware came out which I had hoped would fix the problem.  Now, my watch routinely goes into recovery mode where I have to forget the device, re-pair, and then upgrade to the latest firmware again.  I have contacted support multiple times about the issue and still have not gotten a resolution on the matter.  Again, other people on the forums have had similar experiences.So I really want to give the product 5 stars because when it works, I love it.  It's a nice watch, has the feature set I want, and the price point is reasonable.  The problem is for many users, it just doesn't work.  And their customer service department is completely unable to keep up with the support requests they have coming in.  So unfortunately, I cannot recommend this product in any way.
summary: Constant issues with receiving notifications on iOS

I bought this unit and at first was very pleased - its not got a lot of bells and whistles, but it does work. However, you do have to re-setup to your phone frequently or factory reset the unit and do the initial installation all over again. The so called apps for it are buggy at best.
